utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, I received, just before entering the courtroom, and I've meanwhile read, the verified portion of the transcript and translation. Mr. Tieger, the verification Mr. Stewart asked for has been made available and I have already received three or four lines. Having said this, Mr. Micic, I would like to inform you -- to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Stewart will now continue his examination. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Examined in chief by Mr. Stewart: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, when you entered the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly as a deputy in November, 1990, you were, as you've told the Trial Chamber, a member of a party headed by Ante Markovic. Was there a leader or president of that party for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Nenad Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was a professor where?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the university in Sarajevo. He was the dean of Sarajevo University.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you left SRS party, as you described yesterday, can you -- well, I'll give you the names here. The other three Serb deputies were Mr. Kalinic, Mr. Dodic, and Mr. Peric; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dodik, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Beg your pardon, Dodik. But it was Kalinic, Dodik, and Peric. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They all resigned as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Mr. Kecmanovic? Did he take any corresponding step at that time or did he remain in the party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He remained in the party for a while afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that -- what sort of personal relations did you have with Mr. Kecmanovic before you resigned from the party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing in particular, just the usual.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any problems between you and him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your resignation from the party create any problems or difficulties between you and Mr. Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We simply didn't see each other any more at these meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there -- I'm going to ask you about Tuzla now. Was there at any time a Crisis Staff established by the SDS in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was Vojislav Erkic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the president of SDS in a small settlement near Tuzla. It was called Pozarnica. And he was actually employed in a construction company in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he take any particular steps in 1992 in the light of the developing situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but after he left Tuzla. After they left Tuzla, he tried to organise a Serbian municipality in Tuzla, in Lopare or Bijeljina. At either one of those two places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he tried to organise a Serbian municipality, what do you mean by organising a municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the ambition to organise that, but actually there was a need to help the population that had left Tuzla, for them to accommodate themselves, to start living life - or regular life - again; to settle down, to help those people. It was more of a refugee committee rather than the Municipal Assembly work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any participation in that committee?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called me to these meetings a couple of times for me to try to intervene at the Bijeljina municipality to get them some help, because there were a thousand and one problems with respect to these people. So there was pressure exerted on me to intervene at the Assembly to have that declared as municipality, which was something that I did not accept at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I seek just one clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of your previous answers reads - and you explained that already to some extent - you said, "After they left Tuzla, he tried to organise a Serbian municipality in Tuzla, in Lopare or Bijeljina." When you said "a Serbian municipality in Tuzla" and at the same time you're talking about refugees, was it that he tried to organise a community for those who had left Tuzla in Lopare or in Bijeljina? Is that how I have to understand that? Because otherwise I do not know what you meant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's been clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally ever attend any meeting of any Crisis Staff in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And first -- first of all -- well, if there was more than one, say so, but can you identify what Crisis Staff or Staffs whose meetings you did attend.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Several Crisis Staffs, as far as the Tuzla municipality is concerned. Actually, there was that only one in respect of people who had left Tuzla, and they were trying to get these new arrivals to Bijeljina to fit in, to provide accommodation for them, to make sure their children were going to school; all of these things that have to do with meeting the needs of those people. And they felt that they were not getting enough understanding from the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina, and they wanted my help so that I would intervene with the municipality so that they would receive the help they needed. That was the topic of those meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this the same or something different from what you described a few moments ago in relation to Mr. Vojislav Erkic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same. That's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that Crisis Staff, as you've effectively labelled it there, did that have any other function or purpose apart from the matters which you've just referred to; accommodation, schooling, and so on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it could have had because it didn't really have the means or the conditions to do anything more or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that body receive any instructions or directions of any sort from outside the Tuzla region?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they received any instructions. I tried to have them -- to provide help within the structures of the Bijeljina municipal office, because many of those people didn't have their papers. They were not able to move around freely. These were things that I tried to resolve in some way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in an answer you gave just a few minutes ago, I asked you to identify what Crisis Staff or Staffs there were whose meetings you attended, and you started your answer, "Several Crisis Staffs as far as the Tuzla municipality is concerned." Apart from the body that you've just mentioned connected with Mr. Vojislav Erkic, can you tell the Trial Chamber what other Crisis Staffs you attended?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no other Crisis Staffs there as far as the citizens were concerned, but later some units were formed which were included in the army of Republika Srpska. These were brigades, and these brigades had their own logistical support. There were people there who secured materiel and food for them. So I went to a couple of meetings about that regarding the brigades. I even attended a meeting of that kind in Belgrade at which assistance in food and clothing was sought, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- in 1991 or 1992, did you know anything about any SDA Crisis Staff in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about the existence of a Crisis Staff, because by that time, Tuzla - this was the end of 1991 and the beginning of 1992 - was completely in the hands of the SDA. So according to me, I didn't think that there was any need for an SDA staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in May 1992, you had, you've already indicated, some advance warning or information that there was going to be violence, and you've already said that you eventually left Tuzla. When did you -- in May 1992, when did you first leave Tuzla? I'm talking about either temporarily or permanently. When did you first leave Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May 1992, there was quite intense training and preparations by the Patriotic League in Tuzla. So through certain intelligence services we knew what they were preparing, what they were doing, how far they had come. So in May I left Tuzla with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just stop you there for one moment. Not stopping you from answering the question, but I want you to clarify, please. When you say, "Through certain intelligence services we knew what they were preparing, what they were doing," and so on, who is "we" in that context?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, there was still many people, also in the Muslim Corps and the Croatian Corps, who still believed that there would be peace and that sense would prevail. And we also received information from them, and also even from some officials from the Secretariat of Internal Affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You still haven't quite answered my question as to who was the "we" who received the information.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look. At that time I said that the alliance of reformist forces and the SDP and the League of Communists were still there, present in some way, and they worked. We had good mutual relations. I personally was on good terms with the president of the municipality, with the chief of the SUP, and so on; with all of them. So every day we met and we talked about these events, what was happening, what could happen, what had to be done, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you were telling Their Honours that in May you left Tuzla with your family. Are you able to put a specific date on when you left with your family?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Tuzla on the 13th of May with my wife and one son. One of my sons had already left a year before, for studies in the United States of America. The other son was studying in Sarajevo, and he had come to Tuzla some ten days before that, so my wife, my son, and I left. We left Tuzla. However, I returned to Tuzla on the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so your wife and your son remain in Belgrade, is that right, on the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belgrade, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You returned to Tuzla on the 14th. Why did you return the following day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had promised the then chief, or actually the secretary of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, Mehmed Bajric, that I would come to get his family. So I came back to get his family. So I took his family, his wife and two children, out of Tuzla on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you take them to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Backa Palanka, to their relative's place. Later they came to my place in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is Backa Palanka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbia. Actually in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Bajric himself have any part in your departure, or any active part in your departure from Tuzla with his family on the 14th of May?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He came with his family. They didn't have a lot of luggage. It wasn't a good idea to take a lot of luggage with you at the time because then they would be able to tell that you were leaving town, and that was not very popular, and there were many checkpoints all other the place that were set up by the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you clarify: When you say he came with his family, did Mr. Bajric actually leave Tuzla and also go to Backa Palanka on that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He just took me in his car so that we could pass through without being detained and without having to show my ID. Once we left town, he returned back to town while I went with them to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- on that day, then, on the 14th, from what you'd been hearing, what was your expectation as to what was about to break out by way of violence in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal opinion is that it was because it was so many armed people who were not people with high moral qualities. They were known about town as bad people, and I expected that this would last for two or three days, five days, and then that some kind of authority would be set up. It didn't matter whose or what kind, but I thought that any kind of authority would bring in some sort of order. That is why I believed that we would return after four or five days, because the very fact that my son, my wife and I left with cars, in our shirt sleeves, we didn't bring anything with us. We expected to return in two or three days, so we were thinking we were just going to be out of town until things settled down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear to you that Mr. Bajric shared your expectation that conditions would be suitable for return to Tuzla within a few days?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So far as you knew from whatever sources you had, who were you expecting to attack whom, and what -- between whom did you expect conflict to occur in mid-May 1992 in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps command had already moved out from Tuzla. Only some of the troops remained in the Tuzla barracks. In the Tuzla barracks, there was also a depot of weapons and equipment for the entire barracks, but also this depot housed weapons of the Territorial Defence. According to our information, the TO requested from the army to hand over their weapons. They refused to do so. They wanted to leave the barracks first and then leave the arms behind. I think that they believed the arms would be turned against them, the JNA, that was. Since there was no agreement on that, we had information that the garrison would be attacked and that the attack would last two or three days. We did not expect that there would be a war that would last four years.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said in an answer a few moments ago that you expected that the -- and here I'm paraphrasing or summarising -- the conflict would last for two or three days, five days, and then some type of authority would be set up. That's at page 9, lines 9 to 12 or 13. What -- when you say some type of authority would be set up, what did you have in mind? What authority?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The structures that would remain in town. I had in mind the SDA authority. I did expect them to set up their authority, but I did not expect that it would be so strict. I believed they would restore order in the town, that the barricades would be removed and there would be normal life after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was some -- at that time when you took your family out of Tuzla and Mr. Bajric's family out of Tuzla as you describe, had any sort of deadline been set in Tuzla between the different communities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deadline was never discussed or negotiated. The corps command was General Nedeljkovic, and he was the one who was involved in discussions. I believe that he attended a meeting that I didn't attend. An agreement was signed there and a guarantee was given to the JNA to leave Tuzla with the rest of the troops and arms. All the terms had been agreed on; the deadline, the procedure and everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the agreement, from what you knew, agreement was signed by whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was signed by General Nedeljkovic, his chief of security, Ms. Sulovic, whom I mentioned before; and on behalf of the municipality of Tuzla, all the officials signed: The president of the municipality, the president of the executive board, the chief of the TO of Tuzla, and the chief of the Secretariat of the Interior of the region of Tuzla and of the municipality of Tuzla, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Bajric signed the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was -- did you become aware of any results that these events in mid-May had as far as Serb houses were concerned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're talking about -- I was talking about Tuzla. I should make it clear. What results did you become aware of?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the 15th of May, after this massacre of the convoy that was leaving the town, it was a well-prepared attack. Even the Tuzla television made a footage of that, and I believe that the Tribunal has it at its disposal. Immediately after, that there was the plunder of Serb houses and the apartments were broken into. At that time there were still telephone lines working with Tuzla. We could talk to some people in Tuzla on a daily basis. So I know that my flat had been broken into. The young people belonging to paramilitary formations came into the apartment because they had allegedly seen my son at the window, shooting from a sniper, but this was the same son that had been in the States for a year. But this was not typical only of my apartment. This was the case in 90 per cent of the apartments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when they had allegedly seen your son at the window, you said it was the same son who had been in the United States for a year, where was your other son at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My other son was a student in Sarajevo. He came back early, and on the 13th we moved out together. We had three new cars and we were sure that either the army or the paramilitaries would seize those cars. That's why we wanted to take those cars out and maybe return with the smallest car, the Golf. If they were to take anything, at least they would not have taken our BMW and the Citroen car. They would have taken the Golf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, at the time it was alleged that your son had been seen shooting from the window, was your -- was your son, the one who was not in the United States, was your other son still in Tuzla or was he already in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belgrade. But they didn't mention his name. They mentioned the name of my son who was in America.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is his name?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who is in Belgrade is Nenad, and the one in America is Mladen. But it's -- I don't think that the name mattered to them, whether it was just a guesswork. I don't know whether they knew my son's name or not. They just used one of their names as an excuse to break into the apartment. They did not look for any sniper shooters or sharp-shooters. They just wanted to plunder my apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From where or whom did you get the news that your apartment had been broken into?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Muslim family, the Solkanovici, who resided on the same floor as I did. They raised my sons because both me and my wife worked. Mrs. Solkanovic did not work so we hired her as our helper with our children. She was our private helper, helping us to raise our sons. We were on very good terms with them. They called me and told me. When those people came, the Solkanovics asked them what they wanted and they shoved them away. They said that they saw Mladen shooting from a window and that's why they broke into the apartment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're talking about the month of May, and I would like to know how the JNA was made up. What was the JNA -- what did the JNA look like in Tuzla? Because you stated that military forces had -- were less numerous than before. Can you please give us some explanation about that particular point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Even before that all the troops of Muslim and Croat ethnicity had been withdrawn from the army. However, the officers remained longer, until the date when Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised by the international community, and then they left the military. Until then, they were members of the corps. I believe that General Sadic, who was a colonel at the time, was a very highly ranking officer in the corps. And he was not the only one. Later on, he became the commander of the Tuzla Corps, but the Muslim Tuzla Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In May, if we look at that corps, how many men was it made up of in the barracks you mentioned? Can you give us an approximate figure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Approximately 300 to 400 people. I don't think that there were more. There may have been 30 to 50 active soldiers. The rest were reservists who were helping with the loading of the equipment and ammunition. I don't think that there were many active soldiers. Maybe not more than 50. When I say "active soldiers," I'm referring to the young recruits who were around 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the 13th or the 14th of May, were there still 50 soldiers there or had their number gone down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that they were all there and that from then on there was no opportunity for them to leave. After the 5th or 10th May there was no opportunity for them to leave without an organised escort and a permit to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very sorry, but I'm not satisfied with your answer. I'd like to know how many combatants, how many men there were in those barracks in April, for example, and I'd like to know, if there was indeed a reduction in the number of combatants, I'd like to know how many combatants there were in the barracks on the 12th or 13th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the exact data about the composition of units. However, according to my estimate, there could not have been more than 300 to 350 people. Maybe 400 tops, but that is at the absolute maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on the 12th of May this number had been reduced to about 50 soldiers, so the number went down from 300 to about 50.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Throughout the month of May, from the 1st May onwards, there were not more than 300 to 400 people in the barracks. Their number was a -- was constant. They -- it didn't increase, it didn't diminish until the 15th of May when they agreed to leave. And that is when their number dropped, when they decided to flee, but not earlier than that. There were some brigades, I don't know which one -- which ones were stationed in Tuzla, but when the corps left the barracks, those brigades left with those as well. All those accompanying the corps and the staff of the corps left at the same time. The command of the airport remained, and the complete staff of the airport remained until the 17th or the 18th of May. They left maybe three or four days after the attack on -- on the convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the attack on the convoy, I'd like you to explain exactly what happened. You were not an eyewitness to the attack yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what do you know about the attack? How can you relate this event to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know almost everything about that event. I also saw the TV footage of the entire incident. The entire incident was recorded from one of the skyscrapers by a TV Tuzla crew. I believe that Selim Beslagic also provided comment to that footage, and I believe that the Tribunal has that footage at its disposal. It had been agreed that the rest of the JNA troops, with the equipment and weapons, would leave Tuzla peacefully. The route was agreed on, as well as the timing of their departure. As far as I know, they were to leave about 1.00 in the afternoon. This was prevented. Then they were supposed to leave at 2.00; this didn't happen; and then I believe that they left around 4.30 in the afternoon. And when they reached a curve towards Majevica and Bijeljina, a fire was opened on the convoy. And the convoy consisted of people, explosives, and weapons, and this was insane. All the tarpaulins were down, and you could see that well on the footage. At the head of the convoy there was the president some sort of committee for the national security of Tuzla or the Crisis Staff, whatever you want to call it. We called it differently at the time. His name was Mohamed Brkic [phoen], who had previously been the chief of the regional SUP. I believe that Mehmed Bajric was also there, and they were some sort of a guarantee that the convoy would leave the town safely. They were at the head of the convoy. However, when the convoy reached the mid-point, there was shooting from all sides and the lorries started flying into the air because the explosives had been blown up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was -- I heard in the interpretation that there was fire opened from all sides. Are you saying that there was fire from both sides or from everywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the passage between the residential blocks, and there was shooting from both sides of the residential blocks. Those were machine-gun nests on the buildings themselves, and fire came from both sides.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the number of victims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the official data of the municipality of Tuzla, there was some 15, 16. According to my information that I obtained from the medical centre, there were 204. According to some other information, there was some 168 victims, or maybe 186, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the impact of this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The impact was grave. The town was blocked. After that, you couldn't leave it. It was completely closed and there was a general state of chaos. I believe that the power was taken over by some unauthorised groups of people, groups of plunderers who just started doing whatever they did afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was it who carried out that attack on the convoy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Patriotic League, which had already stationed themselves in Tuzla. They had had some preparations for that around Tuzla. At the beginning, they bore the insignia of the town of Tuzla instead of the customary insignia that the Patriotic League members had in other places. According to my subsequent information, this was carried out on the order of some of my colleagues from the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reformists and our coalition partner; the SDP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned in the course of one of those answers, you said that you believed the Tribunal had the television footage of that incident. Was that an assumption or speculation or do you know specifically something to indicate that the Tribunal has this footage?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the war, an expert analysis of the events that had taken place in Tuzla was carried out, and this was done by the federal prosecutor's office in Belgrade. They collected a lot of material about all that. They spoke to a number of survivors who had been in the convoy, and I saw that material which included the video footage of the convoy and the attack. According to the comment of the then president of the municipality, Selim Beslagic, who had commented upon the incident and the attack and the footage that had been taken from the top of one of the high-rise buildings, and as far as I know, all that has been sent to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could ask if the -- if the Prosecution could -- well, check, first of all. If they tell us, "Yes, we did supply that to you, the Defence, at such-and-such a time," we'll immediately have a look for it in our files. Otherwise, I wonder if the Prosecution, alternatively, would check to see whether this is in fact in the possession of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any idea whether we supplied it. I don't know why we would have, under these circumstances. If there's a specific request for it, I have no objection to making that inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There is a specific request. Your Honour, I was only referring to the possibility that they had already supplied it to us, not to suggest that was likely but to enable the Prosecution to say, "We've already given it to you." That's an option open to them if that's what information is produced. Thank you. I make that request, and I hear Mr. Tieger's response. The -- which is helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, during the period April 1992 up to the time that you left for Belgrade again on the 14th of May, 1992, did you go to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the month of April and May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was -- there was a -- we know, a session of the Republika Srpska Assembly in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992. Did you attend that session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was at the moment when there were intense talks and preparations for the departure of the JNA from Tuzla, and we expected this attack. So I could not attend any meetings of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say when you next went to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a subsequent -- subsequent session, either in June or July. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about subsequent sessions of the Assembly, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in fact I think your answer referred to session in the singular, but that can be checked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you from --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From then onwards in 1992, did you -- I'm talking about the second half of 1992. Did you attend Republika Srpska Assembly sessions with regularity?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain throughout that period living and based in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you would travel down from Belgrade to wherever the Assembly session was taking place; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you normally stay overnight wherever the Assembly session was being held?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you -- you have a brother. You have just one brother, do you, Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what's his name?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Micic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the -- during 1991 and 1992, was your brother living and based in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he have any official position in the SDS in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of the main Municipal Board of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he a deputy in the Republika Srpska Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did he normally attend sessions of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More often than I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you obtain any information from your brother about the existence of a Crisis Staff in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you learn from your brother about a Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in late March or early April there was an armed conflict in Bijeljina between an armed group which called itself the Handzar Divizija, the Handzar Division, and Arkan's unit, which was located on the outskirts of the town of Bijeljina. I don't know many details because at the time I was in the Far East, so that all I know is what I was told. This lasted two or three days, and after that a Crisis Staff or some body was formed that took over administration of the municipality of Bijeljina and did things on its own and stabilised the situation in the town. As far as the Crisis Staff and him personally, I've already said that I had a private company and I happened to have a train of oil derivatives that I was importing through Energoinvest Sarajevo, and this Crisis Staff actually took that. It was about 550 tonnes of diesel fuel and petrol. According to the decision of the Crisis Staff, this was confiscated and distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was a Serb Crisis Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your brother a member of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the -- was it the Handzar Division? What was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that already has a historical significance. From what I know about it, already during World War II the Jerusalem Mufti managed to form in Sarajevo a brigade which was representing the Muslim people at the time, so that the Muslim people would be represented as a people with its own interest. So somebody formed the Handzar Division, which had its first action in Bijeljina. And then recalling the historical events, then there was this other Handzar Division formed in Bijeljina, but this is something I can't really tell you much about because I wasn't living in Bijeljina at the time and the actual incidents occurred when I was in the Far East.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a Muslim body, the Handzar Division; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exclusively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you heard of what was happening in Bijeljina, was there any other specific individual who was actively involved with Arkan in the conflict in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan immediately formed a formation of his own in Bijeljina - I don't know what size - and he appointed Ljubisa Savic, called Mauzer, as its commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time in 1992 receive any communication from your brother which was connected with Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, before the witness proceeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A brief objection. It's simply this: I gather that the information the witness is providing is not from his personal observation but through information he received from others. I've begun to lose the thread of where that information has come from. Presumably a great deal from his brother but I think there should be a greater effort to make clear the provenance of that information. It may lead to objections, it may not, under various circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although the last question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was on my feet before that, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, we are facing some technical problems in the broadcast of this hearing and therefore I was requested to have an early break so that the matter could be fixed. Therefore, we'll have a break now for half an hour, until ten minutes to four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Micic, I had asked you, and I'll repeat the question since we've had a break, did you at any time in 1992 receive any communication from your brother which was connected with Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And first of all, when was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately on my return from that trip. I think it was maybe on the 5th of May or something. No, excuse me. On the 5th of April. I received information that these goods had been confiscated from me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the connection with Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently receive any other communication from your brother which related to Mauzer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that he was with them in this SDS committee, and that was when Arkan promoted some officer and gave him some soldiers to do what he wanted with, and that's when he became the master of Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please make it clear: When who became the master of Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mauzer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever any suggestion in April 1992 that you should go to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was, with certain limitations and warnings that I could be killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from whom did such warnings come?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got warnings from my brother that allegedly Mauzer was looking for me to kill me, that I was allegedly the one who had ruined the Serbs in Tuzla and that this was my fault.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it indicated specifically why you had allegedly ruined the Serbs in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I had led the Serbs astray, that they joined this other party instead of joining the SDS. And had they all joined the SDS, the situation would have been different; that I had created this situation, in a way. Had they all joined the SDS, the situation would have been different.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it appear from these warnings from your brother whether your brother regarded them as something to be taken seriously?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In order to avoid any ambiguity, did your brother regard them as something to be taken seriously?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did take them seriously. Actually, he concealed that from me, and he tried to get me not to come. And then when I did come to Tuzla, actually he took me to all of these locations where he knew they were not. I was actually seeking to have a meeting with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "When I did come to Tuzla ..." was that a slip? Did you mean Tuzla or did you mean Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. I meant Bijeljina. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did you go to Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Bijeljina in mid-April, and I was passing through Bijeljina in that period on my way to Tuzla and back from Tuzla. I would be going through Bijeljina. The serious threats were made after the 15th of May, however. I didn't even know about those threats in April. Sometime on the 5th I landed at Surcin and my son came to pick me up with the car, and I asked him not to come to meet me from Sarajevo. I told him not to come to Tuzla and that I would take a rental car and go to Tuzla. However, he didn't listen to me. He came to Tuzla earlier, and then he went to Belgrade earlier. He actually wanted to have some time to go out in Belgrade. And I think then that on the 5th of April he returned me to Tuzla, and then he could no longer go back to Sarajevo. All the trouble had started already there, and he was not able to go back. So then on the 13th of May, he left Tuzla together with my wife and me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, turning again to the -- to the Serb Assembly that became the Republika Srpska Assembly, when you were present at Assembly sessions, did it ever concern itself with operational aspects of the VRS or the other security forces of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of -- of any involvement by Mr. Krajisnik in any operational aspects of the army or other security or armed forces of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware in 1992 of any Assembly decisions - I'm talking about the Assembly of -- the Serb Assembly, Republika Srpska Assembly - of any Assembly decisions which were contravened or not followed or implemented by the SDS leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know if there were such decisions. There were some minor decisions relating purely to the legal procedure relating to the implementation of decisions at the municipality. If something was not perhaps so easy to implement, perhaps there were reactions to that, but I don't know if there was anything more significant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Djeric, the Prime Minister?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Just as the Prime Minister but not in any other way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any directions or instructions ever given by Mr. Krajisnik to Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there was anything like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware at any time of Mr. Krajisnik giving any instructions or directions to presidents -- SDS presidents of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there were any directives like that either, and I think that that was not within his competencies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik, as president of the Assembly, did he have influence over the deputies in the Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as far as I was concerned. He didn't have any influence over me, but I don't think that he had any influence over any other deputies either.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Krajisnik's standing or reputation among the Serb people in Bosnia generally?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite considerable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what -- are you able to say what the reasons for that were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik had positive charisma because he was consistent and followed laws and wanted to do whatever he was doing properly, with a high degree of quality. He wasn't rushed in the statements that he was making. He was always moderate and considerate, and people liked him and they considered him to be a very serious man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a position to observe how far Dr. Karadzic had influence over Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Krajisnik had influence over Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My private opinion about that is that Dr. Karadzic is somebody who is a very pleasant collocutor. He would listen to whatever you had to say, but in the end he would do whatever he wanted to do. As far as Mr. Krajisnik is concerned, I think that he was more pragmatic, much more realistic in his views, and in all the contacts I had with him, he was like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to observe and form an opinion of General Mladic's attitude towards Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic is an officer, a person of war, a man from that profession who did that job professionally. He was always dissatisfied with the way he was treated, with the attitude of the Assembly towards the army, and he often requested that a state of war be declared, and probably that would allow him more freedom in such conditions and would give him more rights and would give him many more ways to achieve whatever it was that he wanted to achieve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what dissatisfaction did General Mladic appear to have with the way he was treated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, he was always asking the Assembly to vote on laws which would grant more authority and power to the army and would give more power to the army leadership than was provided for under the laws and the constitution. As I said, he wanted to have the state of war declared, which implied the abolition of all the civilian authorities, and it meant that the whole power would be placed in the hands of the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you aware of any consultation of Mr. Krajisnik and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you could call that a consultation. Sometimes they drank coffee together. If that was a consultation, then, yes, but I don't think that that was a consultation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally aware of any instructions or directions being given by Mr. Krajisnik to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said that it was very difficult to give any instructions to General Mladic, if not impossible. So I don't think that Mr. Krajisnik even tried to do any such thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it difficult or impossible for Dr. Karadzic to give instructions to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a while. He even asked for him to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On what grounds?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Disobedience, disagreements. He did not obey the orders that he received from the Presidency. He made his own decisions, I suppose. I don't know any specific reasons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was asked by Dr. Karadzic for the replacement of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, that situation never happened. I believe that they ended up with a rebellion of generals on their hands. Some letters with signatures pledging loyalty to General Mladic arrived. I really don't know who it was who did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What you referred to as rebellion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to take page from my learned friend's book and suggest that it might be helpful to place some of these questions in a time context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One learns from another.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That was -- well, and how flattering it is, Your Honour. I was actually -- that was the very next thing I was going to do, Mr. Tieger will be reassured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- what you referred to as a rebellion of the generals, when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993 or maybe even 1994, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of any support being given by Mr. Krajisnik for the activities of Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, the only support that Arkan enjoyed was from Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred a few minutes ago from -- to General Mladic not obeying orders that he received from the Presidency. In 1992 -- let's -- I'll date this more specifically. In June and July 1992, from your observations, who constituted the Presidency of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official members of the Presidency were Mrs. Plavsic and Professor Koljevic, because they had been members of the BH Presidency in Sarajevo, and they had the legitimacy and -- to continue performing those duties in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period the first half of 1992, is it possible to say who was the most powerful person in the Republika Srpska, or Serb Republic, Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what sense. The military sense, the civilian sense, in a general sense?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, my question is: Is it possible to say who overall was the most powerful person in the Serb Republic, Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In global terms, in the entire territory of Republika Srpska, the highest authority was Dr. Radovan Karadzic. However, the petty power wielders in the municipalities had the most power because they did not obey anybody, and that is why it's very difficult to say who had the most power. If the alleged most powerful person could not issue any orders to the people in the municipalities, then it's very difficult to talk about the supreme power of any one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Let me say I can begin today but I'm going to need a break for couple of reasons. I can articulate them but they include both logistical reasons; secondly, there were matters touched upon that were not specifically addressed in the 65 ter summary; and third, a number of the matters raised anticipated by the 65 ter have either been touched on briefly or not at all, and I need to look a little bit more carefully at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very practical. Would it assist you to have a break now and then would you be better able then to continue, or would you say it makes no difference, I can start now, go as far as I can go and have an early finish today? What would you prefer? Of course, the Chamber would very much like to use the court time as good as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. I think -- I mean, I'll do my best with a break at this point, which I think would be preferable. I think we're going to stay within -- given the difference between the earlier estimates of time and where we find ourselves now, I think we'll be fine for the week, but I'll do my best to proceed after the break, and I'll let the Court know how that's shaping up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we would have a break now, it's now 20 minutes past four, if we would have a break of half an hour, we would restart at ten minutes to five. Then we could not continue until 7.00 because that's too long as far as the technical aspects is concerned. If we would start now, start for the first 20 minutes, then have a half-hour break, then it would be quarter past five and then at least would not be obstructed by technical reasons not to continue until 7.00. I'm not saying -- would that be a solution, that we start now, have 20 minutes? Would you have a programme of questions for the first 20 minutes and then have a break and see where we come today? Because otherwise it's -- it will be the technical aspects that would prevent us anyhow from continuing. It might be the Judges have some questions in between that would bring us to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if I'm hearing the Court correctly, the Chamber would prefer the latter approach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The suggestion would be that we start and at a quarter to five have the first break. So that would require you to fill the first 20 minutes. If you say it's impossible, we're not going to ask the impossible from you, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the Court would give me two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, if that would assist you, if you need to consult yesterday's transcript, I have both today and yesterday open, so if there's any, I would -- as a matter of fact, I would offer the same to the Defence, that if it's a matter of quoting and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I appreciate that, Your Honour. And as the Court can see, I'm setting up for the purpose of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed. Mr. Micic, you will now be -- we will at least make a start with the cross-examination by Mr. Tieger, who is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Among the logistical matters, Your Honour, will be the distribution of certain materials. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. Cross-examined by Mr. Tieger:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, you were asked earlier about the document known as -- or that has been called variously Variant A and B, among other things, asked whether you'd ever heard of it, and you said you had not. Do you know of that document or did you know of that document previously by the name The Instructions Under Emergency Conditions of December 19, 1991, or anything to that effect?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's -- just to make it clear, the question was not specifically whether you heard about it at the time it was issued in December of 1991 or shortly thereafter, but whether you had heard about it before coming to court to give testimony.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this was never voted on, and as far as I know, this was never an item on the Assembly agenda. The first time I heard of that was two days ago when I came here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This Court has had an opportunity to hear evidence about references to Variant A and B at, among other things, different Assembly sessions, including, Mr. Micic, the 46th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. That was held on the 9th through the 11th and 23rd of November, 1994. You've told us that you regularly attended the sessions of the Bosnian Serb Assembly after May of 1992, and in fact, a review of the records of the session held -- 46th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, held in November of 1994, reveals that you were present. Do you now -- and let me tell you, among other things, what was said at that session. During that session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not invite the witness to look at any document. Could I ask you to look at documents when you're invited to do so and to refrain from doing it if you're not invited to do it. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. Micic, to confirm your attendance at that session, if I could ask you to look quickly at tab 11. Tab 11 contains, as you'll see in a moment, certain excerpts from that session. You will see your name recorded there in a couple of places. I'm not going to ask you questions at this moment about those particular passages. I just want you to confirm that you're the Momcilo Micic referred to in those passages.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Karadzic was also present at that session, and he also spoke, and we've had the opportunity to look at his comments on a number of occasions before, but the essence of what he said was when he reminded the assembled delegates of what it was like before the war, spoke about what it was like in municipalities where the Serbs were in a majority and where they were in a minority, and then asked the delegates, "Do you remember instructions A and instructions B," and went on to talk about having Crisis Staffs which clearly knew that they were in power, mentioning that they might have made mistakes but they were the authorities. Thinking back to that session and the comments made by Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Micic, does that refresh your recollection about ever having heard about the document known as Variant A and B before coming to court or before coming to The Hague a couple of days ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I'm not aware of that. Radovan Karadzic may have said it at that Assembly meeting, but I don't know anything about any plan. If he had said it, maybe his words were addressed to somebody else, to be appreciated by somebody else. At that time I was a member of an opposition party, and I didn't hear or understand any of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that you were also present, based on what you've told us before, at the 50th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, held in April of 1995 in Sanski Most. Do you recall that one?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I was there. I may have been, but I'm not sure. I even think that I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And any particular reason why you're able to recall that you were not present at that session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, that's another occasion on which Dr. Karadzic made reference, explicit reference, to the A and B instructions, but if you're not sure you were there, I won't cite that passage for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, before we continue, the tab 11, 46th Assembly session on your list does not bear any exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a mistake or should we assign a number to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My suggestion would be -- yes, I think we probably should assign a number at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let's do it, and you check --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are excerpts, so the number will then be assigned to excerpts of the 46th Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1020, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, earlier today you spoke about the -- what I think you referred to as kind of a refugee committee that was set up by persons who had left Tuzla and gone to Bijeljina for the purpose of organising assistance to others who had left -- other Serbs who had left Tuzla. Did I get that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If -- based on your description, I did not understand that to be a kind of formal government structure established pursuant to orders of some higher body for the purpose of engaging in the governance of the municipality as an alternative to the joint government that had been elected in November of 1990. It wasn't that kind of body, if I understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've understood me correctly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the Variant A and B document provides for the establishment of Serbian municipalities throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina as an alternate structure to the governments, joint governments, that were elected in November of 1990. Was such a body, such a Serbian municipality established in Tuzla in the first few months of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it. I don't think it existed. If it had existed, it would have already left Tuzla as such. There wouldn't have been any pressure on me in the Assembly to fight for the declaration of the Serbian municipality of Tuzla. It would have had some sort of legitimacy if it had been elected, if it had been set up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I didn't -- I wasn't talking about an elected body at open elections. I was referring to a body that was set up pursuant to the instructions of 19 December 1991 to serve as an alternative body to the joint government, an alternative Serb body. But I think you've, in any event, answered my question. And in that respect, let me ask you to look at another document, and that's found at tab 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the list indicates this was previously admitted as P529, Hanson tab 57.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, the document at tab 17 that you're now looking at is a Decision on the Establishment of the Serb Municipality of Tuzla, which was adopted at a session of the Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Tuzla held on 3 March 1992. And as you can see from the prefatory language at the top of the page, that decision was taken pursuant to, among other things, Article 4 of the Instructions on the Organisation and Activity of Organs of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina Under Emergency Circumstances of 19 December 1991. Is it still your testimony, Mr. Micic, that you were unaware of the establishment of a Serbian municipality in Tuzla of this type and specifically one that was established pursuant to the instructions of 19 December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I adhere by that. You have to appreciate that even if this did exist - and I can see that it did - then it was only the SDS that did that. I was in another party. I did not belong to the SDS. There was no effort made to know of these decisions, but I wonder how come, once they left Tuzla, how come they asked me to fight for the proclamation of the Serbian municipality of Tuzla in the Serbian parliament if they had already had this. I've never seen this before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock. And since you -- I suggested that we would have a break at quarter to five, I gave a message to others that we have a break at quarter to five, so I'd like to have a break now and resume at quarter past five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber may have arrived a couple of minutes late. We then still had to wait for another couple of minutes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, just one more question about your awareness of the establishment of a Serbian municipality in Tuzla before we move on to another subject, and in that connection if I can direct your attention to tab -- I think that has to be distributed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then wait for that. Meanwhile, Mr. Tieger, we assigned now a number to tab 11. I hardly can imagine that -- because the reference by Mr. Karadzic to the A and B document at a later stage, it's clear in my memory that we went through that before.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You're quite right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore could you please verify whether it really is something new or something already in evidence, but then perhaps the whole of it instead of just the excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First of all, I think that's a good suggestion, and we will look at that this evening for precisely that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, I want you to turn your attention next to an excerpt from the 18th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, held on August 11, 1992, a session at which the attendance records indicate you were present. And in that connection, I want to direct your attention to the remarks of Mr. Tesic found at page 14 of the English translation. And I believe the interpreters have the benefit of a table which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There are only two pages, so--

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They shouldn't have too much trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it one of the problems might be that -- yes. The English translation -- the original B/C/S starts only halfway the first page of the English, and then -- yes, on the first page, last three digits 623.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On that occasion, Mr. Micic, Mr. Tesic said: "Honoured Presidency, ladies and gentlemen, we brought the decision on establishing the Tuzla municipality on 23 March this year. It was sent by fax on 24 March." He goes on to indicate that, by mistake, the decision wasn't verified by the Assembly placed on the list of municipalities, and then he describes the geographical extent of the Serbian municipality of Tuzla. Does that remind you now, Mr. Micic, about your previous knowledge of the establishment of a Serbian municipality or was that a reference at the Assembly that you simply no longer recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly did discuss the Serbian municipality of Tuzla but what you gave me to read is a statement by a deputy of the SDS who, amongst others, also asked for this to be adopted and for the municipality of Tuzla to be verified. I took that as a personal thing. I thought that some people had their own personal thing or interest in those -- in the Tuzla municipality, but I don't know whether any decision was made later in this period that you are talking about, and I don't know if anything like that was valid. I think that this was just done by somebody on their own initiative. A telex was sent, but what does it mean? Anybody could send a telex to anyone. But I assert that there was no verification at the Bosnian Assembly or the Assembly of the Serbian People to form a municipality of Tuzla, a Serb municipality of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's be quite clear on this, Mr. Micic. Are you suggesting that in the context of 1992 and in the wake of efforts to establish Serbian municipalities, to have them verified at the Assembly, and the evidence indicates that many, many, many Serbian municipalities were established and verified, that you considered each and every one of those municipalities to be simply a personal lark by someone from the region as opposed to an official act verified and adopted by the Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again that this was not a result of any gathering by anyone, any forum or of any body at which this would be adopted and a municipality formed, because I can see here that there was a total of 24 or 23 deputies present, of whom nine were councillors. That's what they were called. The others were presidents of village boards of the SDS who didn't have any legality or legitimacy to be able to do that, and I believe that it was just somebody who drafted such a document in order to promote themselves and to send it somewhere. But I assert that the topic of the agenda of the Assembly was never the formation of a Serbian municipality of Tuzla, at least as far as I know. I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, may I draw your attention to the following: Today a question was put to you. You were asked, "Was such a body, such a Serbian municipality, established in Tuzla in the first few months of 1992?" Your answer was, "I'm not aware of it. I don't think it existed. If it had existed, it would have already left Tuzla as such." And then later on you said, "It would have had some sort of legitimacy if it had been elected, if it had been set up." And then Mr. Tieger said, "I wasn't talking about an elected body," but finally he concluded that you had answered his question that you were not aware of the establishment of a Serbian municipality in Tuzla in early 1992. In your last answer, you told us that the Serbian municipality of Tuzla was discussed at an Assembly meeting, at a Republika Srpska Assembly meeting. The answer to the first question should have included, if you would have answered that question in accordance with the solemn declaration that you gave, should have included that it was discussed at an Assembly meeting but that you are not convinced that this was anything more than any personal project of somebody. So you're invited to tell us as an answer to the questions put to you in this respect, the establishment of the Serbian municipality of Tuzla, to tell us what you know about it even if you personally would have an opinion on whether it was legitimate, yes or no. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well -- and it was my intention to move on to the next subject in light of the time, but I don't want to preclude you from responding to the opportunity presented by the Court, but if you're satisfied with your previous answers, I will move on to the next subject.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that we understood each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, as far as I'm concerned, we did understand each other. I had asked you, Mr. Micic, about your awareness about the establishment of a Serbian municipality; you denied such awareness; I presented you with documentation indicating that it was discussed in your presence. Have I missed something?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm talking about something else. I differentiate between the period in Tuzla up until the 15th of May and after the 15th of May with Tuzla. Not in Tuzla but with Tuzla. Up to May 15th, I don't know whether anybody ever formed the Serbian municipality of Tuzla in Tuzla. I know about attempts to form the Serbian municipality of Tuzla outside of Tuzla after that period, and I explained why and what was the reason for that. The discussion by Mr. Tesic is something that I really don't recall, and I wouldn't be able to comment on it, but I don't think that it's very serious. The fact that somebody sent some telexes, I didn't have access to those telexes. I didn't know that anyone was doing anything. But I assert that the municipality of Tuzla was not verified through the parliament. It was one question. There were a million questions that I didn't really pay that much attention to, so that was one of them. I don't know if you're satisfied with that answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, let's turn to another question. I'd like to direct your attention now to some of the comments you offered in response to questions yesterday about the meeting that you and Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik had with General Jankovic in March of 1992. And -- you indicated --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. Although we're moving on to another topic, I just want to make an observation on the English translation that we were looking at a moment ago, the comments of Mr. Tesic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where it says "Honoured Presidency, ladies and gentlemen, we brought the decision on establishing the Tuzla municipality." That could mislead in English. Mr. Karganovic assures me that the Serbian has a sense of we took or we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
