utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I appreciate you're assisted by Mr. Karganovic in interpreting language. I think it's most helpful for the Defence that there is someone who can read it. If, however, there needs to be a verification in court, I always would like to invite you to put the relevant portion on the ELMO so that the translators can look at it and see whether it's a correct translation, yes or no. That's the procedure I would -- rather than to present first the, I would say the private interpretation, although I fully appreciate, and if I were in your circumstances, I -- as a matter of fact, I still remember how important it was for Defence counsel to be assisted by someone who speaks the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It certainly helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not in any way a criticism, but the way of verifying the correctness of an interpretation should be through our interpreters. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I -- yes. I'm suggesting something and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or it could also be read by Mr. Karganovic. I have no problem with that, since we did --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's such -- I'll do it through the ELMO, if necessary. It's a very -- it's a very tiny point, it relates to one word or one phrase. Mr. Karganovic can certainly read the relevant Serbian phrase, but it -- well, perhaps we'll start way that round, then, Your Honour, if we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll see.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the original and Mr. Karganovic is reading quite fast, and could the original, the B/C/S be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I expected you to have received the same as we have, which is the original. Mr. Karganovic, reading always goes very quick. We have it now on the ELMO. Perhaps you could read it again slowly so that the interpreters can translate it for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, before we begin, I'm a little confused. We've gone to considerable trouble, as the Court is aware, to copy the excerpts in both languages and present them to the interpreters. I thought the interpreters had the original of this excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's really something to be verified after this hearing. It's on the ELMO now. Let me just look at it. And could you please slowly read it, Mr. Karganovic, and the interpreters will then translate it for us. Could we zoom in, perhaps, on the relevant portion, which is the middle of the page. Yes, there we are.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We have found the copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apologies, I take it, Mr. Tieger, are accepted. Could you please read it again, Mr. Karganovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARGANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Honoured Presidency, ladies and gentlemen, the decision on the forming of the municipality of Tuzla was adopted on the 23rd of March."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So "we brought the decision" is that it "was adopted." Yes, that's clear. There is a slight difference in language which might be relevant. Thank you, Mr. Stewart. So I do understand whether it was brought in the Assembly is a different matter, but I take it that you want to draw our attention it was only mentioned that it was adopted at the local level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was -- normally it would -- it would have been such a trivial point. It was actually -- it was the end of the sentence, the reference to it being sent by fax.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That necessitated making it clear whether the translation was brought which would imply some physical taking of a document or adopted in a sense of a decision being made. It was the whole sentence which necessitated clearing up that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's not clear who sent it to whom, although the word "telefax" appears clearly in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may make it crystal clear: What it is, as originally translated in English it could have been read in the sense of -- especially with the reference to being sent by fax on the 24th of March, it could have been understood in the sense of it being physically brought, that a piece of paper had been brought on that day and then the following day sent by fax. It was in order to clear that up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clear now. Let's proceed. Mr. Tieger, we are now back to yesterday, the meeting with -- in the presence of Mr. Jankovic. That's where you stopped, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if I understood your testimony correctly, Mr. Micic, you were -- you conveyed to us a sense that the meeting was a disappointment to you and to General Jankovic and that, as a result, it was your clear impression that thereafter, in light of the fact that no meaningful information had been communicated during that meeting, that there was no further contact or coordination with the Tuzla Corps command and the SDS leadership thereafter. Is that essentially the sense of the meeting and its consequences that you were trying to convey to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my impression at that time. I don't know later if there were any contacts that I was not privy to. I cannot know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't apparent to you from the objective of the meeting and from the substance and tenor of the meeting that there would be further contact between the SDS leadership and the Tuzla Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we turn next, then, to tab 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That document will need a new exhibit number, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 18, Your Honours, will be P1021.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: P1021, found at tab 18, Mr. Micic, is a handwritten letter dated 23 March 1992 from the president of the Serbian municipality of Kalesija, Petar Jankovic, to Minister Ostojic. First of all, for the benefit of the Court, Kalesija is a municipality which is adjacent to Tuzla; is that right? Between Tuzla and Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it you understand the reference to Minister Ostojic to be Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the letter indicates as follows: "Dear Minister, The situation in Kalesija is complex and unpredictable. "The Serbian people are grateful for the material and moral support in these difficult times. "We saw who is loyal and who disloyal. "Political and strategic decisions are being coordinated with the Corps Command and the 4th Armoured Brigade. I wish you success in the creation of the Serbian state in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Micic, is it your testimony that in the aftermath of the meeting between Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, General Jankovic, and yourself, that you were unaware that political and strategic decisions would be coordinated with the corps command and the 4th Armoured Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said clearly that it was my impression that the contact between the corps command and Mr. Radovan Karadzic was during that last meeting, and there was no more need to meet further. But as far as what is written here, I'm not in a position to comment on somebody else's letters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, I submit that you painted a picture of the contact between the corps command and the SDS leadership which strongly suggested that there would be no form of contact or coordination, and that indeed the SDS leadership had no idea whatsoever what they wanted to do. And I submit further that that's quite inconsistent with this letter and the facts as they actually were in March of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who that man is from Kalesija. I don't know him and I don't know what his role is, what his function is, and whether he was in any important position in the SDS. I don't know. I mean, if he was of a -- in a prominent position or stood for something important, I would have known him. This is a private letter. I have to tell you that at that time everybody was organising something around their house. He was probably organising something. I don't know what that was. He was in contact with people. I don't know the man, so I don't know what he wanted to say with this. But to take it as an element that the corps command contacted the SDS through people like this is something that I would consider frivolous on the part of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you did let the witness go. He starts commenting on a letter he sees for the first time, I take it, giving a lot of speculation. As a matter of fact, your question, of course, the issue seems to be that Mr. Micic gave evidence as to the impression he got from his meeting with Mr. Karadzic, and whether that was a right impression or a wrong impression and whether that impression was given or not given is something which is not clarified by this issue. Whether, at least in this letter, someone presents a view that the SDS leadership, or at least the one who is addressed in this letter, which is not automatically the SDS leadership as such, may have had some ideas on how to proceed is, of course, a different matter, and it doesn't assist that much to listen to this interpretation, speculation, commenting on this letter. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, not inviting my response, so I won't offer any to that, but we'll certainly reserve comment on it for the appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If -- of course the Chamber, if -- if you show that it greatly assists us, then of course we'll -- it may become apparent from what is still to come.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, you told us yesterday that at the time of a meeting that you had with Dr. Karadzic after the Serb deputies left the Assembly and before a recognition, that there was no discussion with Dr. Karadzic about the ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have the page references as we go along?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 46 of the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of the meeting -- at the time of the meeting you had with General Jankovic and Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik, was there already discussion of the ethnic division of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the question is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the issue of the ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina current among the SDS leadership and at the Bosnian Serb Assembly in March of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was. I think that you misunderstood me when I spoke about my visit and General Jankovic's visit to General Krajisnik. I said then that I did not get the impression that Radovan Karadzic, as the president of the party, as a person who was already advocating such a policy, could say anything for the microlocality which responded to the area of responsibility of the Tuzla Corps. That was in the domain of General Jankovic. As far as the global plan of the SDS and the Serb deputies in the Assembly was concerned, the division of Bosnia, about some borders and just to -- which was the basis of everything, maintain the equality of the people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because if you lost equality, then you would lose everything. With the adoption of the declaration, the Serbs were practically evicted from that equality. That was the general policy of the SDS and the Serb deputies. Here we mixed up the conversation of General Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Micic, what you actually said about the meeting, found at pages 29 and 30, was that, although you wanted to hear the programme and what the objectives were, as a result of the meeting, "... we understood that there was no programme and there were no objectives." So with that characterisation of the state of affairs in March 1992, I'd like to turn your attention and the Court's attention to a session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly in March of 1992, and in fact on the 18th of March, 1992. That's the 11th session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And those excerpts, I believe, Your Honour, can be found at tab 1. It's a previous exhibit, P64, P65, Treanor, tab 10. It's also a Hanson exhibit, as the list indicates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The page would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The page you're --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll be referring to a number of different pages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Micic, by this time the global goals of the Bosnian Serb leadership that you referred to earlier were in the process of being implemented in the individual municipalities all around Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was the thrust of what was happening in mid to late March 1992, the effort by the Bosnian Serb leadership to actualise the goal of ethnic division on the ground in the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that fair or not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question of global life of Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina was not in dispute. And again I'm talking about the conversation with General Jankovic. These global objectives and positions were not discussed at all. Something else was discussed. And I said what that was. It was the area of responsibility of the corps itself. Naturally, General Jankovic was interested in taking care of the army and preserving them. These were young men, 18-year-olds, and it's clear that he wanted to know how he was to behave at certain points. I will also tell you --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning your attention away from the specific meeting with General Jankovic to the issue of what was happening and what efforts were being made by the Bosnian Serb leadership in connection with moving forward on the global objective of ethnic division, and I'm putting to you that by March 18th and moving on into later March, there was a focus on actualising that process on the ground, on taking power in municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the situation was in other municipalities. I can talk about those municipalities where I resided, where I was. As for the forcible takeover of some municipalities, I personally believe that as long as the JNA was present in the territory of Bosnia, there was no way for doing something forcibly. It was only when the JNA left the conditions were created for those things that you are putting to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's interesting to hear you respond to my question by saying you can only answer in terms of the specific municipalities in which you resided, because the 11th session of the Assembly is one at which the attendance records indicate you were present. So let me turn your attention to the matters that were discussed, at least some of the matters that were discussed, at that very Assembly. And perhaps it's useful if I turn your attention to a number of references and -- before I seek your response to any particular ones. First of all, if I can turn your attention to page 12 of the -- and 13 of the English, which is SA02-5727 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's page 16, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik says, "What is the problem? "I think the problem is that they want Bosnia and Herzegovina to be internationally recognised at any cost. They want it to be a state. "In this respect, it would be good if we could do one thing for strategic reasons: If we could start implementing what we have agreed upon, the ethnic division on the ground. That we start determining the territory, and once the territory is determined, it remains to be established in additional negotiations whose authorities are to function and in what way. I cannot say whether this will be fair in political terms, there is not much fairness in politics after all, and yes, if it does not turn out to be fair, the Serbian people will be blamed. But we cannot accept a state designed in the mind of the SDA people." Turning your attention later in the session to the remarks of Mrs. Plavsic found at pages 17 and 18 of the session. That's SA02-5734, page 23. Mrs. Plavsic first recommends that negotiators in future talks try to arrange that the door is as wide open as possible to connect with Serbian lands, and then she goes on to say: "Regarding what has been said earlier, that this must be made reality on the ground, yes, for sure, but if it could also include a key to such an arrangement in the document, which is certainly going to be modified after the next round of talks," et cetera. Turning to page 22 of the English. That's Dr. Kalinic speaking at page 30. "I offer my full support to all those who want to work on this to the fullest extent possible to establish our authority everywhere we have territory: Starting from the local commune, to the municipality, to the republican level. We should not wait for anyone." And he goes on to note Mrs. Plavsic's explanation. Mr. Bjelovic speaks immediately afterwards, and in the third paragraph of his comment, says: "I suggest that we adopt the Croatian model of creating a de facto situation on the ground, to continue working in the Serbian assembly, and to have the negotiating team carry on their work." Mr. Perisic, later on, at page 27 of the English and page 41 of the B/C/S: "A very important matter and one highlighted by many people, is that a state is created in two ways: By negotiations, talks, diplomatic methods, political moves, etc. The other way, which is more important, entails practical moves on the ground."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Micic, if you are not able to find it immediately, please ask for some more time. So your attention has now been drawn to page 41 of your B/C/S copy. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you said page 41 of the B/C/S, Mr. Perisic talking. In my --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I see on this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On page 40 it's Mr. Ijacic who starts talking --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's either at the bottom of page 37 or the top of page 38. And thank you for pointing that out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, Mr. Tieger made a mistake. Could you please look at the bottom of page 37 and/or the top of page 38.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, it's four paragraphs above the point at which Ms. Subic begins to speak. Do you see that now, that paragraph? And it begins: "A very important matter, and one highlighted by many people ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you found it, Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Perisic talks about the two ways a state is created; one by negotiations, et cetera, and then continues: "The other way, which is more important, entails practical moves on the ground. This is where we are not good enough; we just think that we have control and authority, that we control the territory. Objectively, we are far from it." At page 29 of the English, Mr. Ijacic speaks. This is page 41, immediately before Professor Miljanovic speaks. Do you have that reference, Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he says: "It has been stressed here that the actual situation on the ground was very important, and I would like to add that the more we achieve on the ground, the less will have to be said by our negotiators to achieve more. And secondly, the more we achieve on the ground, the more time will be on our side, and the negotiations can last even longer. In the opposite case, time is our enemy." And finally, let me direct your attention to remarks by Mr. Krajisnik, beginning at page 31 of the English and page 45 of the B/C/S. You will see a portion immediately above some enumerated items where Mr. Krajisnik says: "Allow me one conclusion." Then he begins: "The document drafted at the conference ..." et cetera. Then he continues by saying: "A proposal for the takeover of actual power and establishment of authority in the Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be prepared for the next session." Mr. Micic, does that now refresh or change your recollection about the fact -- I think you indicated before that you were -- didn't recall such discussions. Does that remind you now, or do you at least agree that in mid-March of 1992 that the Bosnian Serb leadership was in the process of moving forward to ensure that those global objectives you mentioned were being actualised on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is beyond dispute that Republika Srpska wanted to have an autonomy, to have some power, but the people -- two people that you're talking about, I don't know who they are, this Perisic and Ijacic. They must have been guests. They were not MPs. They were just guests who intervened and spoke about something. I don't know these people. And since I never respected or listened to the guests, I'm not familiar with their interventions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, you have not been asked here to serve as an interpreter of documents or to be -- to deconstruct the transcripts of the Bosnian Serb Assemblies in the abstract. You're here as someone who lived through these events and purports to have some knowledge of them. You were at this session. You heard the discussions that took place there, including the comments by a variety of people, including Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Krajisnik, and others present there. If you don't have any recollection of what was happening in Republika Srpska in mid-March of 1992, you can simply tell us, but it serves no purpose to quibble about the comments of a couple of people who you didn't know very well when I provided you with a lot of information about the tenor of that meeting and the conclusions of that meeting in order to refresh your recollection, if it is at all possible, about what was happening at that time. Isn't it the case, as I put to you earlier, that in mid-March and late March of 1992 the Bosnian Serb leadership was in the process of ensuring that its global objectives were being actualised in the municipalities around Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was a confirmation of the Cutileiro plan. This was accepted. Yesterday I told you that there had been a lot of negligence in the municipalities and that we wanted to restore some order there, but I don't see what is in dispute here. I still believe that these conclusions are certainly valid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean the answer to my question is yes, or is it no, or is it that you simply don't know what was happening at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the leadership of the then Republika Srpska, if we can call it that, if we can call it a republic, had an objective to create some sort of autonomy that would provide security for the life of the Serbian people in that territory, and that would be that. I personally think that there was not a plan as to what municipalities would be encompassed into that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the succeeding sessions of the 12th, 13th, and 14th Assemblies, held on March 24th - that's the 12th and 13th held on the same day - and March 27th, do you recall that the leadership advised the deputies that the police would be sufficient for the process of taking control in the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was in that sense, that the police would be enough, but I believe that by the virtue of their tasks, the police should have been tasked with providing security in those municipalities. This is the role of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, may I just return to your -- one of your previous answers. You said that you thought that the leadership had an objective to provide some sort of autonomy for the people in that territory. You are confronted with texts, and let me just take the last one you were confronted with, which does not speak about creating some sort of autonomy but talks about a proposal for the takeover of actual power. I take it that autonomy can be established by taking over of power. Not necessarily by taking over power. You can create autonomy in other ways as well. So if you're talking about some sort of autonomy in view of the quote you were confronted with, is that an autonomy which was gained by the takeover of the power or was that an autonomy achieved in any other way? And if it would be in any other way, would you please explain what you had in mind that those who were speaking at this Assembly meeting pointed at.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In simple terms, I was referring to bringing authorities to the areas with a majority Serb population. I believe that authorities had to be established because the authorities had to function. Some order had to be introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ask you, what do you understand the takeover of actual power to be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that power should have been taken over from somebody in a forcible way, because this had been done in a number of municipalities. What I'm referring to is establishing power from the state of lawlessness to going to the state of lawfulness. And I don't think that this means to take over power in a forcible way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the ones who were speaking, at least this quote, seems not to reflect what your opinion is but what the opinion of the speaker is. I mean, I do understand that you had your own ideas about it, but you're asked about what you learned at that time to be the -- what was expressed by those who were speaking in the Assembly and with whose texts you're now confronted. I mean, it doesn't make much sense to say -- if I ask you, What does it mean to take over power, take over actual power? And you say, Well, that's not the way it should have been done, because it was not to take over the power from someone else. But how do you understand these texts? Do they agree with your position that there should be no takeover of power, of actual power?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that you're right. If this is what the transcript says, this must have been said, but what I'm saying is there were all sorts of statements, all sorts of ambitions, all sorts of programmes. We were not very realistic, and I still claim that nobody said that we should go to a municipality and to take over power there but, rather, that some order and authorities should be introduced into the areas where the majority Serb population. This is how I understand these statements. But of course there were statements to the effect that this should be done from Junik down to the very south of Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask another question. This last line reads: "Proposal for the takeover of actual power and establishment of authority in the Republic of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall be prepared ..." Was on the whole of the territory of the Serbian -- Republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina, was there a Serb majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I'm implying is that where the Serbs were de facto in power, this should have been implemented de jure as well. So just to cover, by laws, the de facto situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the proposal was for the takeover of actual power and establishment of authority. That sounds as two things. It don't say a proposal for where the actual power is already in the hands of the Serbs to establish authority. No, it reads, "A proposal for the takeover of actual power and establishment of authority ..." Is that the same or not the same as you just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't think it's the same as what you just explained to us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. I believe that the takeover should have taken place in the areas with a majority Serb population where this had not been done. This is my private opinion. So this is where the takeover should have taken place. And in the other areas, it should have just been implemented de jure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's your private opinion. But the issue is not what you thought about the matter. The issue is about what was said at that time. Is what your private opinion is, is that what was said at the time or is what was said different from what you now express as your opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. My opinion is that this is what was meant when all this was being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand your testimony well if you say what we read here is actually meant to say what you just expressed was your private opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that this is exactly what they, as well, thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, please turn to tab 7. That contains P64, P65 Treanor 16, tab 221; the 34th Assembly session held in August, September, and the 1st of October 1993. That's the 27th to 29 August, 9th and 10th September, and 29th of September and the 1st of October, 1993. Mr. Micic, please turn to remarks by Mr. Mladic at page 66 of the English. I will give you the B/C/S reference in a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if you're looking where page 66 of the English appears in B/C/S, I think it would be on page 65, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the beginning of General Mladic's remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's, from what I see, where he says, "Distinguished chairman." I find that at one-third of page 65.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 65.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, as you can see, General Mladic says, shortly after his remarks begin: "First, people and the army, with the help from the rest of us according to our possibilities, have carried out the most of tasks, and strategic goals, set to them. We have created Republika Srpska." What were the strategic goals that General Mladic and the army -- that were set to General Mladic and the army and which they carried out that resulted in the creation of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember this speech by General Mladic. I think that I also discussed something at that Assembly session. I remember it. But I must tell you that the Assembly of Republika Srpska, or at least the leadership of Republika Srpska, according to what I know, was never in a situation of stating clearly what it was that it wanted, what was the minimum, the maximum, or what was the optimum. This is something that I was always remarking upon, both to the leadership and to the Assembly. I think that the leadership of Republika Srpska never laid down any objectives for the simple reason that they never knew decisively to say what they wanted. What Mladic said here is something that I felt was just the boasting of a general. I don't know why we were talking about the creation of Republika Srpska, but it is true that he did fight. He was fighting. Battles were being waged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when General Mladic referred to the strategic goals set to the army, you had no idea what he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army often talks about strategy, so probably this term "strategic goals" was also something that he used in that sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that was an intra-army reference by General Mladic, and you as a civilian politician didn't have any idea what he meant by that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, actually, in answer to your question, yes, I had no idea.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's your testimony to this Chamber, Mr. Micic, you had idea what the strategic goals were? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Strategic goals that were laid down, adopted. I don't know whether that was set ever. I never heard of any programme or a plan of strategic goals when we're talking about territory. When we're talking about the equality of peoples and the division, okay, there was that. I don't know what is considered to be included in the term "strategic goals."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me mention a couple of the strategic goals to you. The first of the strategic goals, Mr. Micic, was the separation of the other nations in Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Serbs, the ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Ever heard of that as a strategic goal of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnia-Herzegovina was like a leopard skin. It was all mixed. To tell you again, I never heard of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you come to answer the question. The question was whether you ever heard of this as a strategic goal. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention, then, to pages 14 and 15 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tieger, I interrupted the witness when he said, "I never heard of," but let the witness first then complete his answer. You said you never heard of ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying again that I never heard of any strategic goals adopted as some sort of project or goal or programme. I don't know of anything like that. As to whether there were any statements made and demands being put, and even, I think, in this discussion I proposed something about the division of Bosnia. There were such things, but this was never adopted, and it was never valid that that was that, or at least I never know -- I never knew that anything like that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then tell us about strategic goals that were never adopted or were invalid. What could you tell us about invalid and non-adopted strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were demands to have a division carried out. There were different discussions. And I told you yesterday that there were people who were very difficult in these positions. There were even statements that they did this or that, that they were boasting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me say the following: This Chamber has received evidence that suggests the existence of six strategic goals, the first one mentioned to you by Mr. Tieger. Now, irrespective of whether they were adopted or whether they were valid or not, do you have any idea about what the five other strategic goals of which this Chamber received evidence would be about; from what you heard, statements, whatever source, I do not mind. Could you fill in any of the remaining five strategic goals as they were until now presented, true or not, to this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the period that you are talking about and in which this Assembly session took place, at that time I never knew or heard about strategic goals. I heard of strategic goals the day before yesterday, and I read them, and I know what they are, but I didn't know of them, nor was I present at the Assembly session when they were discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. So you heard about strategic goals for the first time two days ago. Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, when I came here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I direct your attention to pages 14 and 15 of the English, page 12 of the B/C/S. These are the remarks of Dr. Karadzic at this same session, the 34th session. Dr. Karadzic says: "Strategic goals adopted by this Assembly have been or will be achieved to the fullest extent, just to remind those who do not know it. This Assembly reached strategic goals of Serb people, which have become, in a certain way, our tasks, our obligation to realise them, but those were the goals we aimed at and the goals we aim at now to achieve whenever it would be possible." And then Dr. Karadzic goes on to enumerate the strategic goals. "Consequently," he says, "the first goal was to separate us, to keep our independence and avoid foreign domination. In other words, to create our state product in the former Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. "The second goal is to have connected territories - we have called them a corridor, and that is to have connected territories in Posavina. "The third goal is to let the river of Drina be never more a border between Serb people. "The fourth goal is that the valley of the river of Neretva, that is the left bank of Neretva, is to belong to east Herzegovina and/or Republika Srpska due to the historical and ethnic right, geographical and economic right, et cetera. "The fifth goal is to maintain our part in and protect our rights to Sarajevo, because that part is very important for integrating the territories of east Herzegovina, Old Herzegovina and Romanija and because our interests in concentrating education, culture, science and economy are met in this valley. "Thus, that interest is to create Serb Sarajevo, whatever it is to be called, but to create it out of the Serb territory in the town of Sarajevo. "The sixth goal is to have an exit to the seaside." And then Dr. Karadzic goes on to discuss the fifth and sixth and fourth some more. I can also tell you, Mr. Micic, that at pages 128 through 132 of the same session, later on, Mr. Krajisnik goes on to discuss and enumerate the strategic goals again, all six of them, in quite some detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, you were not being honest or candid or forthright with this Court when you said that you only heard of the strategic goals for the first time two days ago. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I see that it says so here and that that's it, however, I didn't know that that was adopted by the Assembly. I still don't know that today. I see here that Radovan Karadzic said that this was adopted by the Assembly. I don't know when the Assembly adopted that. I just thought that, you know, he was simply enumerating his ideas about that. I didn't think it was anything else. I'm just saying that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, I earlier asked you to tell us about what you knew about strategic goals, valid or invalid, adopted or not adopted. Now it seems that you're saying, "Well, I heard about it but I thought they were not valid or they were not adopted." I invited you five minutes ago to tell us what you knew about strategic goals, whether or not valid, whether or not adopted, and now you tell us that you heard about them but you thought they were not valid. As you say, "I still don't know --" "I see that it says there and that's it, however, I did not know that that was adopted by the Assembly. I still don't know that today. I see here that Radovan Karadzic said that this was adopted by the Assembly. I don't know when the Assembly adopted it." Now, a simple question: Did you hear what Mr. Karadzic said - yes or no - about the strategic goals? Did you hear him explaining about the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably did listen to him, but this was 13 or 14 years ago, and I really don't know that strategic goals were discussed at that time. At least, I don't remember that. I don't remember anyone talking about strategic goals as some kind of programme. I simply understood that as their address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What you now say, at the very end, is that what may have been said perhaps in your presence in the Assembly you may have forgotten about it. So it's not that you say, "I for the first time in my life heard about it two days ago," but, "I heard about it two days ago, and when I heard any earlier about it I must have forgotten it." Is that how we are to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two days ago I heard about that for the first time as a strategic programme or a strategic goal. Two days ago was the first time that I encountered some programme of strategic objectives. I did not register that as strategic goals earlier. I didn't register it as any programme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that this record says that Mr. Karadzic says, "Strategic goals adopted by this Assembly have been or will be achieved." I mean, he was thinking in terms of strategic goals, of a programme. You have missed that or did you hear that at the time, but did you, despite this language, not consider that to be a programmatic issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I asked you whether it was one or the other, so yes is not -- I asked have you missed that or did you hear that at the time, but did you, despite this language, not consider that to be a programmatic issue. Which one of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure that I even heard it. Had I heard it, I would probably remember it, but I really do not remember it. I assume that -- well, maybe I don't know even if I was in the hall at that particular time. Perhaps I wasn't. I really don't remember that part of the address.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you say you don't remember. Judge Hanoteau has some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you did not present those pages of the 34th session which represent the words of Mr. Krajisnik, and the Chamber would appreciate it if you would confront the witness not only with the presentation of the strategic goals by Mr. Karadzic and a short reference made by General Mladic but also how this was done by Mr. Krajisnik. And since this session took place over several days, we can see that you're referring, I think, to page 124 or something like that, which is not in tab 7, and tab 7A starts at page 128. And I think you were referring to 124, but I should check that. Perhaps you can -- otherwise, you prepare it -- otherwise, you prepare it for tomorrow, perhaps, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe it's in tab 7A, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: However, there is another reference I'd like to get to before we conclude today. I don't mind at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether immediately or at a later moment, the Chamber would like you to confront the witness with that portion of the ... May I then take it 7A is -- I have to look at it -- yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness can turn to tab 7A. It's page 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. Micic. Mr. Krajisnik says, in the second sentence: "I would like to ask you to keep in mind the first strategic goal, and that is to divide and take our share out of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to create our own state." And he goes on about the other strategic goals which are not less important. The second strategic goal is the corridor. On page 129 of the English he says the third strategic goal was Drina. About two or three sentences later, the fourth strategic goal is Neretva and Una. The next paragraph he talks about Sarajevo. And finally, on page 130 of the English, after that lengthy discussion -- find the reference. At the -- approximately ten lines up from the bottom of page 130 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can we be sure that Mr. Micic is also picking up these passages as we go along?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the paragraph that begins: "We consulted with municipality presidents." About five sentences after that, Mr. Krajisnik says, "That is our strategic goal, I have to remind you when we were accepting these goals," and he goes on to say, "none of us thought at the time that we would get exit to the sea."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you find it, Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, I put it to you again that you were not being honest with this Court when you said you only heard of the strategic goals two days ago and that in fact you knew long before then that they were adopted on the 12th of May by the Assembly. You knew what those goals were as well as the territories those goals were supposed to encompass. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you again that I didn't consider that to be a programme at the time, or even two days ago, as a programme of the way in which Republika Srpska was to be formed. All of this was said, but I just personally took it to be just a speech with these phrases being used. But I really do not recollect any strategic goals being in any kind of programme, and that is what I kept actually criticising the Assembly for, that way of life, because there was no rules, and now it turns out that all of this was happening but I was criticising it. So what was I criticising, then?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct or incorrect that you were well aware of the goals long before you came to The Hague two days ago as well as the territories those goals were supposed to encompass?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying again I do not recall any strategic goals. Probably it was there but I didn't know. There were probably more demands than this but I didn't know about them. I didn't know there was any kind of plan or programme made until two days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to turn quickly then to the next exhibit before we adjourn, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You have two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then I'd like to distribute -- I may need slightly longer than two minutes but I'm going to show a video and I'll show the last portions of that, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the interpreters and the technicians would consent.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's find out if we have that leeway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not hear any -- otherwise, we have to do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I thank the interpreters very much for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You certainly need to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, we're about to watch portions of a broadcast entitled "An Open Screen," which is a talk with you and Mr. Maksimovic on February 7th, 1995. And in the interests of time, I want to turn to the last three clips of that tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, for the benefit of the Court and interpreters, the last three are found beginning at midpoint on page 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I have to oppose Mr. Dodik because they had an independent dialogue in the studio. He said we don't stand a military chance. A long time ago, in the first year of war, Mr. Karadzic said that we did not want to defeat Muslims and he would say this in the public and before the RS Assembly. This has remained our position even today. But, the six principles you mentioned, or six strategic goals rather than principles, strategic goals adopted by our Assembly on 12 May 1992 in Banja Luka, those include Sarajevo as well. At that time, we counted our own part of Sarajevo, naturally, the part we believe we have the right to have, and we have the right to a considerable part of the Sarajevo territory, both in the city centre and even more so in its surroundings."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was Mr. Maksimovic who was talking, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Let's hear Professor Maksimovic to tell me how in what way we can realise our strategic goals. Is war the only option or does this include negotiations toward something else? Do we have a programme or a project of solutions for our strategic goals?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Of course I would like to give an answer at least partially to the question put by Mr. Micic. The strategic goals we adopted were adopted at a time when Mr. Micic also shared my views. Those goals were defined based on our assessments, on our estimates in May 1992. In my view, we have partly accomplished these goals. We failed to accomplish due to reasons I cannot go into right now, but they have essentially remained up to now, and Mr. Micic is well aware of those goals as well as the territories those goals are supposed to encompass. I'm not of those people who should here go into what way and how or talk about other people's competencies."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, we have two parts of the transcript, being the line where Mr. Micic is supposed to say, "Which I still do," and later on where Mr. Micic is supposed to say, "Correct," have not been translated by the interpreters. Perhaps because they didn't hear it. Of course, it might be of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We can certainly play that last portion again, Your Honour, and ask the -- I also noted that at least the last response by the -- on the tape was rather quiet, but certainly audible and visible, and I ask the translators to watch that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we acknowledge that those two points are there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If that helps to short circuit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that certainly short circuits the matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, that was you who said, "Correct," when Mr. Maksimovic said to you, "And Mr. Micic is well aware of those goals as well as the territories those goals are supposed to encompass"; isn't that right? We can see that you weren't out of the room, you could see what was happening, and that you acknowledged the goals; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This discussion was held in Pale, in the Pale studio. This was when a witch-hunt took place against us who were not members of the SDS. Pressure was put on us constantly to join the SDS or at least not to be their opposition, and in my view this should have been presented to the general public, to portray us as people who were against Republika Srpska, who were meant to destroy Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Micic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will answer that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about answering the question of Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did accept that as a figure of speech, but again I claim I did not know anything about the strategic goals. Since Professor Maksimovic said it, I accepted it formally, and I confirmed it, but I still believe that Maksimovic spoke about the strategic goals in the same way, just figuratively, but the whole purpose of that was entirely different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that your last question for today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't want to abuse the interpreters' --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- tolerance and patience any further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn for the day, and -- we will adjourn for the day. We will resume tomorrow morning [sic], quarter past two in this same courtroom. And I'd like to instruct you, Mr. Micic, not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given or you are still about to give in this courtroom. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
